messages.content:
You translate a user's question about land and climate into a plan in the query language below. Reply with the plan only: one JSON object that follows the language exactly, with no other text.

# Query language

A plan is one JSON object with exactly these keys:

```
{
  "area": "<study area name from the catalogue>",
  "land": {"classes": ["<class>", ...], "min_patch_ha": <number or null>},
  "near": [ {"classes": ["<class>", ...], "distance_m": <number>, "negate": <true|false>}, ... ],
  "climate": [ <condition>, ... ],
  "output": "map" | "area"
}
```

Meaning. The answer is the set of pixels (30 m) that satisfy every part (logical AND):

- `land`: pixels of any of the listed classes (land as mapped for the catalogue's land year). If
  `min_patch_ha` is a number, keep only connected patches of these classes at least that many hectares.
- `near`: one entry per distance rule. `negate: false` keeps pixels within `distance_m` metres of any pixel of
  the listed classes; `negate: true` keeps pixels that are NOT within that distance. Use `[]` if none.
- `climate`: one entry per NASA POWER climate condition (see below). Use `[]` if none.
- `output`: `"map"` to show the pixels; `"area"` when the question asks how much land (hectares).

A climate condition:

```
{
  "variable": "<variable from the catalogue>",
  "years": [<first year>, <last year>],
  "months": [<month numbers 1-12>],
  "stat": "mean" | "total" | "days_above" | "days_below",
  "day_threshold": <number, only for days_above / days_below, else null>,
  "test": <test>
}
```

For each year in `years`, the stat is computed over that year's days in `months` (all within one calendar
year): `mean` of the daily values, `total` (sum) of the daily values, or the number of days whose daily value is
strictly above / below `day_threshold`. The condition's value is the average of these yearly values over
`years`. It is computed for each NASA POWER grid cell (about 50 km) and applies to every pixel in that cell.

The test is one of:

- `{"kind": "absolute", "op": ">=" | "<=", "value": <number>}`: compare the value with a number (in the
  variable's units, or days for `days_above`/`days_below`).
- `{"kind": "history_rank", "side": "high" | "low", "pct": <0-100>, "history": [<first year>, <last year>]}`:
  the cell's value is among the highest (`high`) or lowest (`low`) `pct` percent of that cell's own yearly
  values for the same months over the `history` years. Use this for "one of the wettest / driest / hottest
  10% of springs since 2001" and similar comparisons with a place's own past.
- `{"kind": "area_rank", "side": "high" | "low", "pct": <0-100>}`: the cell's value is among the highest or
  lowest `pct` percent of the study area's cells. Use this for "the sunniest half of the study area" and
  similar comparisons between places.

Examples.

"Show cropland within 100 m of a wetland in the North Dakota study area." ->
`{"area": "north_dakota", "land": {"classes": ["cropland"], "min_patch_ha": null},
  "near": [{"classes": ["wetland"], "distance_m": 100, "negate": false}], "climate": [], "output": "map"}`

"In the North Dakota study area, how much hay land had a June 2015 that was one of the 25% hottest Junes
(mean daily temperature) since 2001?" ->
`{"area": "north_dakota", "land": {"classes": ["hay"], "min_patch_ha": null}, "near": [],
  "climate": [{"variable": "T2M", "years": [2015, 2015], "months": [6], "stat": "mean", "day_threshold": null,
  "test": {"kind": "history_rank", "side": "high", "pct": 25, "history": [2001, 2025]}}], "output": "area"}`


# Catalogue

Land is mapped for 2024. Climate data are daily, 2001-2025.

Study areas:
- `north_dakota`: North Dakota study area (Prairie Pothole farm country)
- `north_carolina`: North Carolina study area (eastern Piedmont and Coastal Plain, many solar farms)
- `minnesota`: Minnesota study area (farm country with solar farms)
- `georgia`: Georgia study area (Coastal Plain and Piedmont, solar farms)

Land classes (the same in every area):
- `corn`: corn (maize)
- `soybeans`: soybeans
- `spring_wheat`: spring wheat
- `sunflower`: sunflower
- `canola`: canola
- `cotton`: cotton
- `other_crop`: annual crops not listed separately
- `hay`: hay land: alfalfa and other hay
- `grassland`: grassland and pasture (grazing land)
- `fallow`: fallow or idle cropland
- `forest`: forest (deciduous, evergreen, mixed)
- `developed`: developed land (buildings, roads, towns, open developed space)
- `water`: open water
- `wetland`: wetlands (marsh, wet meadow, wooded wetland)
- `solar_farm`: existing utility-scale solar farms (built by the land year)
- `cropland`: any annual crop (all crops below plus other annual crops)

Climate variables (NASA POWER):
- `T2M`: air temperature at 2 m, daily mean (C)
- `T2M_MAX`: daily maximum air temperature at 2 m (C)
- `T2M_MIN`: daily minimum air temperature at 2 m (C)
- `PRECTOTCORR`: rainfall / precipitation (mm per day; use stat total for mm over a period)
- `GWETROOT`: root-zone soil wetness (0 = dry to 1 = saturated)
- `WS50M`: wind speed at 50 m (m/s)
- `RH2M`: relative humidity at 2 m (%)
- `ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN`: sunlight: all-sky solar radiation at the surface (kWh per m2 per day)
- `GDD10`: growing degree days, base 10 C (degree-days per day; use stat total for a season's sum)
- `HDD18`: heating degree days, base 18.3 C (degree-days per day; use stat total for a sum)
- `CDD18`: cooling degree days, base 18.3 C (degree-days per day; use stat total for a sum)
- `LOW_WIND_SUN`: 1 on a low-wind, low-sun day (50 m wind and sunlight both in the cell's lowest 10% of days), else 0 (use stat total to count such days)
In the North Carolina study area: Towns and built-up land with the hottest summer in 2022

We need to translate the user's request into the query language.

User: "In the North Carolina study area: Towns and built-up land with the hottest summer in 2022"

Interpretation: They want built-up land (which is class "developed") in North Carolina, and they want those pixels that had the hottest summer in 2022. "Hottest summer" likely refers to mean temperature over summer months (June, July, August) being among the highest compared to some history? Or just the hottest summer in 2022 relative to other years? The phrase "the hottest summer in 2022" could be interpreted as "the summer of 2022 was the hottest (i.e., highest mean temperature) among the years considered". But they might want the hottest summer of 2022 (i.e., the summer of 2022 itself) - but that seems trivial: it's just the summer of 2022. Usually they'd ask "with the hottest summer in 2022" meaning "the summer of 2022 was the hottest (i.e., among the hottest)". Could be they want to select pixels where the summer 2022 temperature is among the highest (e.g., top 10%?) but they didn't specify percentile. Could be they just want the summer 2022 temperature condition: "hottest summer in 2022" meaning the summer of 2022 was the hottest compared to other years, but we need a test. Since no percentile given, maybe they want the absolute hottest summer (i.e., highest mean temperature) among all years 2001-2025? But they only mention 2022. Could be they want to filter for the summer of 2022 being the hottest (i.e., compare to history). Could use history_rank with side "high", pct maybe 0? Not allowed. Could use absolute test: maybe they want the mean temperature in summer 2022 to be >= some threshold? Not given.

Given ambiguous, we need to produce a plan. Probably they want to select developed land and then filter for summer 2022 mean temperature being among the highest (maybe top 10%?) but not specified. Could default to "high" relative to history, maybe top 10%? But we shouldn't guess a percentile. The simplest is to use a history_rank test with side "high", pct 100? That would include all. Not helpful.

Maybe they just want the summer 2022 mean temperature condition, but no test. The language requires a test. Could use absolute with some placeholder? Not allowed.

Maybe they want "the hottest summer in 2022" meaning "the summer of 2022 was the hottest (i.e., highest mean temperature) among all years for that location". That is a history_rank test with side "high", pct 0? Actually to be the highest, it must be in the top 0%? Actually top 0% would be none. Could use pct 0.1? Not defined.

Better to interpret as "the hottest summer (i.e., highest mean temperature) in 2022" meaning they want the mean temperature for summer 2022 (June, July, August) and maybe they want to output the map of developed land with that temperature condition? But they didn't specify a threshold.

Given the instructions, we must produce a valid JSON. We need to fill climate condition with a test. Perhaps we can use absolute test with a placeholder like >= 0? That would be always true, but still valid. But that would not reflect "hottest". However, the user didn't give a numeric threshold.

Maybe we can interpret "hottest summer in 2022" as "the summer of 2022 was the hottest compared to other years, i.e., rank high". So we can use history_rank with side "high", pct 10 (top 10%). That seems reasonable.

Thus climate condition: variable T2M, years [2022,2022], months [6,7,8], stat "mean", day_threshold null, test: {"kind":"history_rank","side":"high","pct":10,"history":[2001,2025]}. That selects cells where the 2022 summer mean temperature is in the top 10% of summers from 2001-2025.

Output: maybe they want map. The question: "In the North Carolina study area: Towns and built-up land with the hottest summer in 2022". Likely they want a map. So output "map".

Thus final JSON:

{
  "area": "north_carolina",
  "land": {"classes": ["developed"], "min_patch_ha": null},
  "near": [],
  "climate": [
    {
      "variable": "T2M",
      "years": [2022, 2022],
      "months": [6,7,8],
      "stat": "mean",
      "day_threshold": null,
      "test": {"kind": "history_rank", "side": "high", "pct": 10, "history": [2001, 2025]}
    }
  ],
  "output": "map"
}

Return only that.
